title: HTTP API design: methods, status codes, pagination, and errors
description: Many APIs called REST are really RPC over HTTP. This quiz covers the choices that matter once other developers build against your endpoints: safe and idempotent methods, `PUT` vs. `PATCH` vs. `POST`, idempotency keys, cursor vs. offset pagination, what 409, 412, 422, and 429 mean, versioning, and error formats a client can parse. Most answers point to the relevant spec (RFC 9110, RFC 5789, RFC 9457).

questions.title: Which of these HTTP methods are idempotent?
questions.description: Idempotent means that sending the request once or many times leaves the server in the same state.

options.text: `GET`
`POST`
`PUT`
`PATCH`
`DELETE`

questions.explanation:
RFC 9110 §9.2.2 lists `PUT`, `DELETE`, and all safe methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`) as idempotent. `POST` isn't idempotent. Two identical `POST`s usually create two resources. `PATCH` isn't guaranteed to be idempotent either (RFC 5789 says so directly), because a patch can describe a relative change.

The usual trap is `DELETE`. A second `DELETE` may return `404` instead of `204`, but idempotency is about the resulting state (the resource is gone), not the status code.

questions.title: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be "safe"?

options.text: The client asks for no state change, so the method is essentially read-only (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`)
Repeating it any number of times leaves the server in the same state
The server guarantees the method has no side effects at all, including logging
The method may only be sent over HTTPS

questions.explanation:
RFC 9110 §9.2.1 calls a method safe when "its defined semantics are essentially read-only; i.e., the client does not request, and does not expect, any state change on the origin server."

Two things people often mix up:

- Safe and idempotent are different properties. "Same state after N calls" is idempotency. `DELETE` is idempotent but not safe, because it changes state. `GET` is both.
- Safe methods can still have side effects. The spec allows a safe request to write a log line or bump a counter. The client didn't ask for those effects, so it "cannot be held accountable" for them.

questions.title: You want to change a user's `email` and leave every other field alone. Which method fits best?
questions.description: The full user representation is large.

options.text: `PATCH`, sending only the fields to change
`PUT`, since it's the standard update method
`POST`, creating a fresh representation of the user
`GET` with the new email in a query parameter

questions.explanation:
`PATCH` (RFC 5789) applies a partial change, which is exactly the one-field case.

The others don't fit:

- `PUT` replaces the resource (RFC 9110 §9.3.4). Its body is the complete new state, so a `PUT` that leaves out fields asks the server to clear them. You can wipe data you meant to keep.
- `POST` asks the resource to process the body by its own rules, often to create something. It doesn't say "modify this existing resource."
- `GET` is safe and read-only. Using it to change data breaks the uniform interface, and caches or crawlers could trigger writes.

questions.title: Why is `PATCH` not guaranteed to be idempotent, while `PUT` is?
questions.description:
Take this JSON Patch (RFC 6902) request body:

```json
[{ "op": "add", "path": "/items/-", "value": "sku-9" }]
```

options.text: A patch can describe a relative change. Here `/items/-` appends, so replaying it adds `sku-9` again, while `PUT` sends the whole representation, so repeats end in the same state
`PATCH` always sends less data than `PUT`, and smaller requests are never idempotent
`PATCH` is unsafe, and no unsafe method can ever be idempotent
Intermediaries cache `PUT` but not `PATCH`, and that caching is what makes `PUT` idempotent

questions.explanation:
In JSON Patch, the path token `-` means "append to the array." Applying the patch once gives `items: [..., "sku-9"]`. Sending the same request again gives `items: [..., "sku-9", "sku-9"]`. Two sends produce two different states, so the request isn't idempotent. RFC 5789 says plainly that PATCH is "neither safe nor idempotent."

`PUT` is idempotent because it carries the entire target state. Sending it N times leaves the resource the same as sending it once.

A specific `PATCH` can still be idempotent, for example one that only sets absolute values. The method doesn't promise it, though, so clients and intermediaries can't assume it.

questions.title: A `POST /charges` request times out before the response arrives, and the client retries. How do you prevent a double charge?
questions.description: The first attempt charged the card, but the response was lost, so the client can't tell whether it worked.

options.text: The client sends a unique `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the first result under that key and returns the stored response for any retry with the same key, so the card is charged once
Switch the endpoint to `PUT`, since `PUT` is idempotent and `POST` is not
Nothing, because TCP guarantees each request runs at most once
Return `409 Conflict` on the retry so the client gives up on the charge

questions.explanation:
`POST` is neither safe nor idempotent, so retrying it can repeat side effects. An idempotency key makes an unsafe operation safe to retry. Stripe popularized the pattern, and the IETF now has a draft header for it. The client generates one key per logical operation and sends it on every retry. The server saves the outcome under that key and returns the saved response for repeats instead of running the operation again.

Why the other answers fail:

- `PUT` is idempotent because the client chooses the target URI. When the server assigns the new charge's identity, changing the verb doesn't tell it that two requests are the same charge.
- TCP delivers bytes in order on one connection. It knows nothing about retries over new connections, so it can't give exactly-once behavior at the application level.
- `409` throws the result away. The client still doesn't know whether the money moved.

If a client reuses a key with a different request body, the server should reject it (commonly with `422`), so each key maps to exactly one operation.
questions.references: [Stripe: Idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) · [IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/)

questions.title: An infinite-scroll feed reads from a table that keeps growing. Users must never see a duplicate or miss an item, and page 10,000 must load as fast as page 1. Which pagination design fits?

options.text: Cursor (keyset) pagination. Return an opaque cursor holding the last row's sort key, and fetch the next page with `WHERE (created_at, id) < :cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n`
Offset/limit pagination, because it lets the user jump to any page number
Offset/limit with a bigger page size to cut the number of requests
Shuffle the table randomly on each request to spread the load

questions.explanation:
Keyset (cursor) pagination starts each page from the last item's sort key, which is stable and indexed, instead of from a row count. That gives you two things:

1. Deep pages stay fast. `WHERE (created_at, id) < :cursor LIMIT n` is an index range scan that jumps straight to the right spot. `OFFSET 200000` makes the database read 200,000 rows and throw them away first.
2. Pages stay stable while data changes. A value defines the window, not a count, so inserts and deletes elsewhere don't shift it and cause skips or duplicates.

The cost, and the reason the offset answer is tempting, is that keyset pagination can't jump to page 137. It also needs a unique, fully ordered sort key, which is why `id` breaks ties on `created_at`.

questions.title: Which of these are real drawbacks of `OFFSET`/`LIMIT` pagination that keyset pagination avoids?

options.text: Rows can be skipped or returned twice when items are inserted or deleted between page fetches
Deep pages get slower because the database scans and discards every skipped row
It cannot return rows in any sorted order
Clients lose the ability to jump directly to an arbitrary page number

questions.explanation:
The first two are real. Here's the drift with a page size of 2, sorted by `id` descending. Page 1 (`OFFSET 0`) over `[10, 9, 8]` returns `10, 9`. Then row `11` arrives. Page 2 (`OFFSET 2`) now runs over `[11, 10, 9, 8]`, skips `11, 10`, and returns `9, 8`, so `9` shows up twice. A deletion before the window causes a skip instead. And `OFFSET n` costs O(n), because the engine walks past and discards the first `n` rows.

The other two are false. Offset pagination works fine with `ORDER BY`. Jumping to any page number is something offset can do and keyset can't, so it counts in offset's favor.
questions.references: [Use The Index, Luke: We need tool support for keyset pagination](https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)

questions.title: Your API handles optimistic concurrency with a `version` field in the request body. A client sends `version: 3`, but the stored resource is already at `version: 5` because someone else updated it first. The request has no `If-Match` header. Which status code fits?

options.text: `409 Conflict`
`412 Precondition Failed`
`400 Bad Request`
`404 Not Found`

questions.explanation:
`409 Conflict` (RFC 9110 §15.5.10) means "the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource." A stale version that your application detects is exactly that.

The difference from `412` matters here. `412 Precondition Failed` is for failed HTTP conditional headers like `If-Match` and `If-Unmodified-Since`. In this case the version check lives in the request body and your application code, so `409` is the right signal. `400` is for malformed requests, and this one is well formed. `404` would suggest the resource doesn't exist.

questions.title: A client sends a conditional update with `If-Match: "v5"` to avoid lost updates, but the resource's current `ETag` is `"v7"`. Per RFC 9110, which status code must the server return?
questions.explanation:
`412 Precondition Failed` (RFC 9110 §15.5.13) means a condition in the request headers "evaluated to false when tested on the server." Here's the flow. The server sends an `ETag` (a version fingerprint) with the `GET` response, and the client echoes it in `If-Match` on its next write. If the stored `ETag` no longer matches, someone changed the resource in the meantime. The precondition fails, and the server returns `412` instead of overwriting the newer state.

This is optimistic concurrency built into HTTP. Compare it with the previous question: a version check through an HTTP conditional header gets `412`, and an application-level conflict without one gets `409`.

questions.title: A client `POST`s well-formed JSON to create a user, but `email` is `"not-an-email"` and fails validation. Which status code is most precise?

options.text: `422 Unprocessable Content`, because the syntax is valid but the content fails validation
`400 Bad Request`, because any client error in the body must be a `400`
`500 Internal Server Error`
`409 Conflict`

questions.explanation:
`422 Unprocessable Content` (RFC 9110 §15.5.21) is for when "the server understands the content type ... and the syntax of the request content is correct, but it was unable to process the contained instructions." In other words, the JSON parsed, but a validation rule rejected it. RFC 9110 moved `422` into core HTTP and renamed it from "Unprocessable Entity."

`400 Bad Request` fits malformed syntax, such as invalid JSON or a missing required structure. Some APIs use `400` for every client error, and that's a reasonable house style. If you want to separate "I couldn't parse this" from "I parsed it and it's wrong," `422` is the standard code for the second case. `500` would blame the server, and `409` means a state conflict rather than bad input.

questions.title: A client goes over its rate limit. Which status code should the server return, and which header tells the client when to try again?

options.text: `429 Too Many Requests`, with a `Retry-After` header
`403 Forbidden`, with a `Retry-After` header
`429 Too Many Requests`, with a `Location` header
`503 Service Unavailable` for every throttled client

questions.explanation:
`429 Too Many Requests` (RFC 6585 §4) is the status code for rate limiting. The response "may include a `Retry-After` header indicating how long to wait before making a new request." `Retry-After` is the standard way to tell a client to back off, and it takes either a number of seconds or an HTTP date.

`403 Forbidden` means the client isn't allowed to do this at all. `Location` points to a redirect target or a newly created resource and says nothing about retry timing. `503` says the whole service is unavailable. Sending it to one client that went over quota misleads other clients and confuses load balancers.

questions.title: Which response change is backward compatible, so you can ship it to existing clients without a new API version?

options.text: Adding a new optional field to the JSON response body
Removing a field that clients read
Renaming `created` to `createdAt`
Changing `id` from a JSON number to a string

questions.explanation:
Adding an optional field only adds data. Under the tolerant reader principle, well-behaved clients ignore fields they don't recognize, so they keep working. The principle applies Postel's Law: "be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept."

The other three are breaking changes. Removing, renaming, or retyping a field will crash or misparse existing clients, so each one needs a new major version. If you design for additive changes and document the contract, you can put off `/v2` for a long time and save version bumps for changes that really are incompatible.

questions.title: Per RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs), what media type goes in the `Content-Type` header of a JSON error document?
questions.explanation:
RFC 9457, which replaces RFC 7807, defines a standard error format so every endpoint reports failures the same way. The JSON form uses `application/problem+json` and has members like these:

```json
{
  "type": "https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit",
  "title": "You do not have enough credit.",
  "status": 403,
  "detail": "Your balance is 30, but the cost is 50.",
  "instance": "/account/12345/msgs/abc"
}
```

`type` is a stable URI that clients can branch on. `title` is a short human-readable summary. `status` repeats the HTTP status, and `detail` and `instance` describe this particular occurrence. There's also an XML version, `application/problem+xml`. With one standard format, clients write a single error parser instead of one per endpoint.

questions.title: An API returns HTTP `200` for everything and signals failure with `{ "ok": false }` in the body. What's the main problem?

options.text: Clients, caches, proxies, and monitoring use the status code to tell success from failure, so sending every error as `200` hides failures from standard tooling
It wastes bandwidth because `200` responses are larger on the wire than `4xx` ones
HTTP forbids a response body on `200` responses
Servers are unable to log `200` responses

questions.explanation:
The status code is part of HTTP's uniform interface, and a lot of tooling reads it. Client libraries throw on `4xx` and `5xx`, retry logic backs off on `5xx`, caches store `2xx`, and dashboards alert on error rates. If every error comes back as `200`, errors disappear from monitoring, retries never fire, and every client has to parse the body just to learn whether the call worked.

A better design pairs an accurate status code with a structured body, such as RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`. Infrastructure acts on the code, and the body carries the details. The other options are false: a `200` can have a body, it isn't larger on the wire, and servers log it like any other response.
